Field studies of the Southern big-eared mouse (Loxodontomys micropus) in the temperate forests of southern South America have provided detailed insights into its early life history. Newborn pups are remarkably altricial, with a wet weight at birth of only 2 grams [Wwb = 2 grams]. This tiny neonatal mass necessitates a period of intensive maternal care, during which the offspring are entirely dependent on milk. The weaning process, marking the transition to nutritional independence and solid food, occurs relatively swiftly. Available data indicate that the time since birth at weaning is approximately 12 days [tx = approximately 12 days], by which point the pup has grown to a wet weight of approximately 9.4 grams [Wwx = approximately 9.4 grams], a brief suckling period that is consistent with the rapid developmental pace observed in other small-bodied cricetid rodents inhabiting seasona at a temperature of 37.4 °C [T = 37.4 °C]l environments. This accelerated weaning schedule may be an adaptation to the short austral growing season, allowing females to minimize the interval between successive litters and maximize annual reproductive output in a habitat where resource availability is temporally constrained.

As the weaned juveniles begin their growth trajectory toward adulthood, significant somatic changes occur before the onset of reproductive competence. The wet weight at puberty, representing the body mass at which individuals typically attain sexual maturity, has been recorded at 48 grams [Wwp = 48 grams]. Achieving this mass represents a substantial increase from the weaning weight, reflecting a period of rapid tissue accumulation. The time since birth at puberty is 60 days [tp = 60 days], a milestone that marks the completion of the juvenile growth phase and the commencement of active gametogenesis and the potential for first breeding at a temperature of 37.4 °C [T = 37.4 °C]. This relatively short maturation period facilitates a fast life-history strategy, enabling young born early in the breeding season to potentially contribute to reproduction within the same favorable season, thereby increasing the species' intrinsic rate of increase in productive years.

Adult body size in Loxodontomys micropus exhibits considerable individual variation, with ultimate wet weight spanning a typical range from 45 to 105 grams. The asymptote of the growth curve, representing the maximum recorded adult body mass, centers around 90 grams [Wwi = around 90 grams]. This size places the species within the medium-small cricetid guild of the Patagonian forests. Reproduction in this species is tightly linked to this body size and the prevailing ambient conditions. When considering the maximum potential reproductive rate under optimal conditions, females have been observed to produce litters ranging from four to five pups per litter [N_R_i = four to five pups per litter]. This moderate litter size is balanced by a capacity for rapid sequential breeding events, with approximately one litter produced each year [F_R_i = approximately one litter produced each year], a reproductive frequency that allows for substantial annual recruitment.

Gestation in the Southern big-eared mouse, reflecting the intrauterine development of its altricial young, proceeds over a defined period. Respirometry trials, conducted at the species' normal thermoneutral body temperature of 37.4 °C [T = 37.4 °C], have measured a basal metabolic rate of 97.8 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 97.8 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This metabolic cost must be met before and during gestation. The gestation time is 24.5 days [tg = 24.5 days], a duration that is typical for a rodent of its body size at a temperature of 37.4 °C [T = 37.4 °C]. Following this short pregnancy, the female gives birth to a litter of altricial neonates. The high energetic demands of lactation, which follow this gestation period, are supported by the female's elevated metabolic capacity, ensuring that the rapid growth of the pups from their birth mass to weaning is adequately fueled. This tight coordination between maternal metabolism and offspring development is a hallmark of small mammalian life histories in seasonal environments.

Longevity records for Loxodontomys micropus, compiled from both mark-recapture studies and captive maintenance, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 5.4 years [am = approximately 5.4 years] at a temperature of 37.4 °C [T = 37.4 °C]. This relatively extended lifespan, when considered alongside its rapid maturation and high fecundity, places the species on the slower end of the fast-slow continuum for small mammals, potentially reflecting the buffered, predictable resource base of its forest habitat. At the reference body temperature of 37.4 °C [T = 37.4 °C], the combination of a brief weaning period of 12 days and a 60-day interval to puberty yields a generation time that enables rapid population turnover when conditions are favorable. Comparative analyses with other sigmodontine rodents suggest that this particular suite of life-history traits—moderate litter size, high annual fecundity, and a multi-year reproductive window—represents an adaptive compromise between the pulsed resource availability of temperate forests and the selective pressures of predation from avian and mammalian carnivores.
